sections.title: Basic Statistics (Measures of Central Tendency)
sections.content: Mean (average) is the sum of observations divided by the total number. Median is the middle value when data is sorted. Mode is the most frequently occurring observation. Empirical relation: Mode = 3*Median - 2*Mean.

sections.title: Measures of Dispersion
sections.content: Dispersion measures how scattered data is. Range = Max - Min. Variance (σ²) is the mean of the squares of deviations from the mean: (Σxi²)/n - (Mean)². Standard Deviation (SD or σ) is the positive square root of Variance.

sections.title: Classical Probability
sections.content: Probability of an event E is P(E) = (Number of favorable outcomes) / (Total number of possible outcomes in the sample space). 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. P(Not E) or P(E') = 1 - P(E).

sections.title: Mutually Exclusive vs Independent Events
sections.content: Mutually Exclusive events cannot happen at the same time: P(A ∩ B) = 0. Independent events mean the outcome of one doesn't affect the other: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B).

sections.title: Mathematical Reasoning Basics
sections.content: A 'Statement' is a declarative sentence that is either true (T) or false (F), but not both. Questions, exclamations, and commands are NOT statements. Example: '2 is an even number' is a statement.

sections.title: Logical Connectives
sections.content: AND (∧): True only if BOTH are true. OR (∨): True if AT LEAST ONE is true. NOT (~): Reverses the truth value. IMPLIES (→): False ONLY when True implies False (T → F is F). IFF (↔): True if both have the SAME truth value.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Confusing mutually exclusive with independent events in probability.
2) Assuming standard deviation can be negative (it is always the positive square root).
3) In logic, incorrectly assuming that T → F is True. (A true premise cannot lead to a false conclusion).

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 1 establishes the definitions. Master the basic probability formulas, calculating mean and variance, and constructing basic truth tables for logical connectives.

tricks.title: Addition Theorem Shortcut
tricks.explanation: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B). If the word 'OR' is used, it means Union (∪). If 'AND' is used, it means Intersection (∩).

tricks.title: Probability Complement Rule
tricks.explanation: Whenever a question asks for the probability of 'At least one', ALWAYS use 1 - P(None).
tricks.example: P(at least one head in 3 coin tosses) = 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - P(TTT) = 1 - (1/8) = 7/8.

tricks.title: Variance Calculation Shortcut
tricks.explanation: Instead of subtracting the mean from every observation, use the formula: Variance = Mean of squares - Square of mean.

tricks.title: Logic 'OR' Trick
tricks.explanation: An 'OR' (∨) statement is like parallel circuits. Current flows if any switch is closed. It is False ONLY when both inputs are False.
tricks.example: F ∨ F = F. All other combinations yield T.

tricks.title: Logic 'AND' Trick
tricks.explanation: An 'AND' (∧) statement is like series circuits. Current flows only if all switches are closed. It is True ONLY when both inputs are True.
tricks.example: T ∧ T = T. All other combinations yield F.

tricks.title: De Morgan's Laws in Probability
tricks.explanation: Direct translation from Set Theory: P(A' ∩ B') = P((A ∪ B)') = 1 - P(A ∪ B). And P(A' ∪ B') = P((A ∩ B)') = 1 - P(A ∩ B).
tricks.example: Probability of neither A nor B = 1 - Probability of (A or B).
